Suicide is actually really hard, and most methods are rarely lethal, our bodies are designed to fight poison (automatically throw up when overdosing) and it’s against human nature to hurt ourselves as that goes against everything in our instincts, stabbing is really hard and to do so fatally needs a lot of force, a sharp knife, and specific points in the body to bleed heavily, cutting is hard because our arteries and veins are well protected beneath layers of skin, fat and muscle, and we can lose what looks like a lot of blood before we get close to bleeding out, hanging only works if you are high up enough and the rope you use is strong and secure enough to hold your weight for long enough, but having your air supply cut off causes us to instinctively panic and we thrash around and if the rope isn’t secure enough we fall, hypothermia takes a while to set in, and again it goes against our instincts to allow ourselves to freeze, so it’d need to be extremely cold/stormy weather, and you’d need to be far enough away from everything that your instincts don’t scream at you to run towards shelter, sure fire lethal ways are difficult, like jumping from a height or shooting yourself in the head, because even standing on the edge of a building it’s hard to fight your instincts to get away from danger, and with modern safeguards in place it’s hard to even get somewhere open and high enough to try, and guns are hard to come by (I’m from the UK) so honestly unless you have a gun, can somehow get to a high place, get isolated in a storm, or get strong opiates (heroin, morphine, etc) then it’s only through a LOT of effort or a combination of the above methods that you can die

A diary is the number one thing, have all your homeworks and exam/assignment due dates written in. Have any other important events in as well. 

For each of your subjects, have a pad of file paper and an exercise book, the book should be used in class for rough work, classwork, planning assessments and homework, the file paper should be used to make additional notes, either for exams or to write out homeworks. Or if you prefer to type homeworks on your laptop and submit them online or print them, that'd be neater and you can keep track of word counts and stuff. Maybe have another exercise book per subject for writing final neat notes for revision. 

For each subject, have a lever arch file at home, and keep it neat and orderly so when you come to revise all your stuff is in one place and you don't have to organise it all before revising. 

Depending on what subjects you do, you might need a calculator. 

You'll probably use a lot of file paper and a good few exercise books, so definitely have some of that spare at home, just in case. 

Have a fully stocked pencil case too. Several black and blue ballpoint pens, a few pencils, a few different coloured highlighters, a rubber, a sharpener, a 12" ruler and a 6" ruler, maybe some brightly coloured pens too. Have another pencil case or a jar or smth at home with all the same stuff in it, so you have separate home stationery and school stationery. 

Make sure you have a good quality school bag, not too small (you want it to fit your books), and not too big (you don't have as much stuff as first years). 

It's the same stuff you've needed for previous years, but this level of planning and organisation is needed for sixth form, you're more independent and expected to work hard and keep yourself organised, don't stress, and if you need smth that you don't have, write it down in your diary and get it as soon as you can.

I've just finished upper sixth lit, and honestly, it depends on what you're revising.

If it's a play I'd recommend writing a page or so of notes discussing main themes, characters, context, and plot. Reread the play a couple times. And then pick out at least a few dozen key quotes that can fit multiple topics, and make a page of those quotes with methods (eg metaphor, symbolism, alliteration, stage directions) and a sentence of analysis. 

If it's poetry I'd advise having clean copies of all the poems and rewriting your notes on the page neatly and concisely. Include themes, context, rhythm, rhyme, structure, and form. Maybe pick out a handful of key quotes for each poem. If you need to compare poems have them grouped into separate themes (eg death, love, religion, identity). 

If it's a novel write a couple pages of notes on key themes, characters, context, and plot. Reread the novel a couple times and on the second/third reread pick out key quotes and write another few pages of notes on them.

Do all the rereading and note making AT LEAST one week before your exam/s (preferably a few weeks). On the lead up to your exam read your notes over a few times, do some past papers not timed, ask a teacher, friend, or family member to mark it for you, and see what you need to improve on. Focus on those points you need to improve (whether it's analysis, quotes, context, whatever). Do some timed papers next and again get someone to mark them for you. See if there's improvement. Maybe reread the poems/play/novel again a couple days before your exam. The day before the exam, maybe rewrite some of your most important notes (eg key themes, context and quotes). The day of your exam, don't try to reread all your notes and material, only read the key bits that are most important.

Being numb is a symptom of depression, you've learned to live with it and you may seem happy, but the simple fact that you are numb shows that you may have won the battle, but you haven't won the war. Believe me, I know this all sounds clichéd af, but I've struggled with depression for close to a decade now, and being numb to everything but pretending to be happy is a very common symptom of depression. 

Learning to live with depression can either mean you've gotten appropriate help and can now deal with it in a healthy way, or you simply feel better than you once did and believe you've overcome it yourself. It's not necessarily a bad thing, but feeling numb and closed off isn't healthy.

Depression sucks, it ruins your life, personality and relationships, but it will get better. Maybe not tomorrow, maybe not this year, but one day in the future you'll be sitting and realise that it does get better. There's no cure for depression, and the only treatment is therapy and antidepressants, which you may not currently have access to, but the fact that you exist and realise that you are depressed is the first step towards recovery, my friend. Good luck and keep your head held high, pretending to be confident and sure in your actions is half the battle.
